Proof of Nobori’s generalized Böttcher–Wenzel inequality conjecture

Shuo Shi Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Computational Science, Hunan Key Laboratory for Computation and Simulation in Science and Engineering, Key Laboratory of Intelligent Computing and Information Processing of Ministry of Education, Xiangtan University, Xiangtan, Hunan, 411105, China    Juan Zhang ††thanks: Corresponding author. E-mail: shishuomath@foxmail.com(Shuo Shi); zhangjuan@xtu.edu.cn (Juan Zhang). This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (12671450) and the National Key Research and Development Program of China (2023YFB3001604) Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Computational Science, Hunan Key Laboratory for Computation and Simulation in Science and Engineering, Key Laboratory of Intelligent Computing and Information Processing of Ministry of Education, Xiangtan University, Xiangtan, Hunan, 411105, China
Abstract

Let m,n≥2m,n\geq 2. For m×nm\times n complex matrices AA, CC and an n×mn\times m matrix BB, Nobori (Linear Algebra Appl. 725 (2025) 135–144) proposed the following conjecture on the generalized Böttcher–Wenzel inequality:

‖A​B​C−C​B​A‖F2≤2​‖B‖22​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2,\left\lVert ABC-CBA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2},

where ‖⋅‖F\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{F} is the Frobenius norm, ‖⋅‖2\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{2} is the spectral norm, and ‖⋅‖(2),2\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{(2),2} is the (2,2)(2,2)-norm defined by ‖X‖(2),2=σ1​(X)2+σ2​(X)2\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{(2),2}=\sqrt{\sigma_{1}(X)^{2}+\sigma_{2}(X)^{2}}, in which σ1​(X)\sigma_{1}(X) and σ2​(X)\sigma_{2}(X) are the largest and second largest singular values of XX, respectively. This paper proves the conjecture and, as a consequence, establishes the Kronecker product inequality that Nobori derived from it. In addition, we show that for each fixed m,n≥2m,~n\geq 2, the constant 22 is sharp. We also give necessary and sufficient conditions for equality, namely, the equality condition in the Böttcher–Wenzel inequality and some matrix identities derived from a fixed singular value decomposition.

Keywords: Generalized commutator; Böttcher–Wenzel inequality.

2020 MSC: 15A45, 15A60, 15A18.

1 Introduction

Let Mm,n​(ℂ)M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}) denote the vector space of all m×nm\times n complex matrices. In particular, for m=nm=n, we write it as Mn​(ℂ)M_{n}(\mathbb{C}). Let InI_{n} denote the identity matrix of order nn, and let 𝟎\mathbf{0} denote the zero matrix of a proper size. For X∈Mm,n​(ℂ)X\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}), the conjugate transpose of XX is denoted by X∗X^{*}. Let X∈Mm,n​(ℂ)X\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}). If m≥nm\geq n, then the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of the positive semidefinite matrix X∗​XX^{*}X are called the singular values of XX. If m<nm<n, then the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of the positive semidefinite matrix X​X∗XX^{*} are called the singular values of XX. Let σ1​(X)≥⋯≥σr​(X)\sigma_{1}(X)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{r}(X) denote the singular values of XX with r=min⁡{m,n}r=\min\{m,n\}.

The vector space Mm,n​(ℂ)M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}) is equipped with the usual inner product (X,Y)=tr⁡(X​Y∗)(X,Y)=\operatorname{tr}(XY^{*}) (where tr⁡(Z)\operatorname{tr}(Z) denotes the trace of Z∈Mm​(ℂ)Z\in M_{m}(\mathbb{C})), which satisfies (X,Y)=(Y,X)¯.(X,Y)=\overline{(Y,X)}. For X∈Mm,n​(ℂ)X\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}), the Frobenius norm is given by ‖X‖F=(X,X)\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{F}=\sqrt{(X,X)}; the spectral norm is defined by ‖X‖2=σ1​(X)\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{2}=\sigma_{1}(X); and the (2,2)(2,2)-norm is defined by

‖X‖(2),2=σ1​(X)2+σ2​(X)2.\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{(2),2}=\sqrt{\sigma_{1}(X)^{2}+\sigma_{2}(X)^{2}}.

When a matrix has at most one singular value, we set σ2​(X)=0\sigma_{2}(X)=0.

For A,B∈Mn​(ℂ)A,B\in M_{n}(\mathbb{C}), the inequality

‖A​B−B​A‖F2≤2​‖A‖F2​‖B‖F2\left\lVert AB-BA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{F}^{2} (1)

is given in [1, 2, 5, 9, 12]. Indeed, the upper bound in (1) can be replaced by the following sharper bound [1, 5]:

‖A​B−B​A‖F2≤2​‖A‖(2),22​‖B‖F2.\left\lVert AB-BA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (2)

In particular, Cheng, Fong, and Lei [3] gave necessary and sufficient conditions for equality in (2). In recent years, attempts have been made to generalize the Böttcher-Wenzel inequality (1) by extending the ideas of commutators and norms [4, 10]. In a different direction, estimates have also been studied for the Frobenius norm of a matrix formed from the product and difference of three real square matrices [8]. Nobori [11] also proved the following result: Let A,C∈Mm,n​(ℂ)A,C\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}) and B∈Mn,m​(ℂ)B\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}). Then

‖A​B​C−C​B​A‖F2≤2​‖C‖22​‖A‖(2),22​‖B‖F2.\left\lVert ABC-CBA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

When m=1m=1 or n=1n=1, Nobori gave a stronger estimate with constant 11. Moreover, Nobori proposed the following conjecture [11, Conjecture 3.1].

Conjecture 1.1.

For all A,C∈Mm,n​(ℂ)A,C\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}) and B∈Mn,m​(ℂ)B\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}) with m,n≥2m,n\geq 2,

‖A​B​C−C​B​A‖F2≤2​‖B‖22​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\left\lVert ABC-CBA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (3)

In fact, Nobori [11] showed that (3) always holds when m=1m=1 or n=1n=1. Nobori also proved [11] that Conjecture 1.1 implies the following inequality:

‖A​B​C−C​B​A‖F2≤‖B‖22​‖A⊗C−C⊗A‖F2,\left\lVert ABC-CBA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert A\otimes C-C\otimes A\right\rVert_{F}^{2}, (4)

where X⊗YX\otimes Y denotes the Kronecker product of XX and YY.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives some definitions and lemmas. Section 3 provides a complete proof of the conjecture, which also shows that (4) holds, and demonstrates that 22 is the optimal constant for any fixed m,n≥2m,n\geq 2. Section 4 gives necessary and sufficient conditions for equality in (3).

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we present the idea for proving Conjecture 1.1 and give some concepts and lemmas needed for the proof. If one of the matrices AA, BB, and CC is the zero matrix, then (3) always holds, and equality holds as well. Therefore, throughout this paper, we assume that none of AA, BB, and CC is the zero matrix. Next, we rewrite (3) in an equivalent form.

Lemma 2.1.

Let m,n≥2m,n\geq 2, A,C∈Mm,n​(ℂ)A,C\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}), and B∈Mn,m​(ℂ)B\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}). Then (3) holds if and only if

‖Φ⁡(D)‖F2≤2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2,\displaystyle\left\lVert\Phi(D)\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}, (5)

where D=B‖B‖2D=\frac{B}{\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}}, Φ⁡(Z)=A​Z​C−C​Z​A\Phi(Z)=AZC-CZA.

Proof.

Since BB is not the zero matrix, DD is well defined. In fact, we have B=‖B‖2​DB=\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}D. So

A​B​C−C​B​A\displaystyle ABC-CBA =A⁡(‖B‖2​D)​C−C⁡(‖B‖2​D)​A\displaystyle=A(\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}D)C-C(\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}D)A
=‖B‖2​Φ​(D).\displaystyle=\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}\Phi(D).

Hence,

‖A​B​C−C​B​A‖F2=‖B‖22​‖Φ⁡(D)‖F2.\displaystyle\left\lVert ABC-CBA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\left\lVert\Phi(D)\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

This proves the equivalence. ∎

We note that ‖D‖2=1\left\lVert D\right\rVert_{2}=1. Hence, instead of working with a general matrix BB, we work with a contraction matrix DD, whose standard definition is given below.

Definition 2.2.

[6] A matrix X∈Mn,m​(ℂ)X\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}) is a contraction if ‖X‖2≤1\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1.

For square matrices, the fact that a contraction is a convex combination of unitary matrices is standard; see Zhang [14]. However, a non-square contraction matrix can still be written as a convex combination of isometries or coisometries. We build on this through the following definitions and facts.

Definition 2.3.

[7] A matrix Q∈Mn,m​(ℂ)Q\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}) is called an isometry if Q∗​Q=ImQ^{*}Q=I_{m}, and a coisometry if Q​Q∗=InQQ^{*}=I_{n}.

Remark 2.4.

If QQ is an isometric matrix, then for any X∈Mm,n​(ℂ)X\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}),

(Q​X)∗​(Q​X)=X∗​X.(QX)^{*}(QX)=X^{*}X.

Thus, Q​XQX and XX have the same nonzero singular values, possibly with additional zero singular values. Hence,

‖Q​X‖F=‖X‖F,‖Q​X‖(2),2=‖X‖(2),2.\displaystyle\left\lVert QX\right\rVert_{F}=\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{F},~\left\lVert QX\right\rVert_{(2),2}=\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{(2),2}. (6)

Similarly, if QQ is a coisometric matrix, then

‖X​Q‖F=‖X‖F,‖X​Q‖(2),2=‖X‖(2),2.\displaystyle\left\lVert XQ\right\rVert_{F}=\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{F},~\left\lVert XQ\right\rVert_{(2),2}=\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{(2),2}. (7)
Lemma 2.5.

If m,n≥2m,n\geq 2, A,C∈Mm,n​(ℂ)A,C\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}), and Q∈Mn,m​(ℂ)Q\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}) is an isometric or coisometric matrix, then

‖A​Q​C−C​Q​A‖F2≤2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\left\lVert AQC-CQA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.
Proof.

If QQ is an isometric matrix, then by (6),

‖A​Q​C−C​Q​A‖F2\displaystyle\left\lVert AQC-CQA\right\rVert_{F}^{2} =‖Q⁡(A​Q​C−C​Q​A)‖F2\displaystyle=\left\lVert Q(AQC-CQA)\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
=‖(Q​A)​(Q​C)−(Q​C)​(Q​A)‖F2\displaystyle=\left\lVert(QA)(QC)-(QC)(QA)\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
≤2​‖Q​A‖(2),22​‖Q​C‖F2​(by (2))\displaystyle\leq 2\left\lVert QA\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert QC\right\rVert_{F}^{2}~(\text{by~\eqref{eq:BW}})
=2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\displaystyle=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

If QQ is a coisometric matrix, then by (7), we apply the same estimate to

(A​Q​C−C​Q​A)​Q=(A​Q)​(C​Q)−(C​Q)​(A​Q).(AQC-CQA)Q=(AQ)(CQ)-(CQ)(AQ).

∎

When BB is an isometry or a coisometry, (3) holds. This is important for proving (3). However, to explicitly write a non-square contraction matrix as a convex combination of isometries or coisometries, several results are still needed. The first is the singular value decomposition [13, 14].

Theorem 2.6.

Let X∈Mn,m​(ℂ)X\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}) and r=min⁡(m,n)r=\min(m,n). Then there exist two orthonormal sets

{u1,…,ur}⊆ℂn,{v1,…,vr}⊆ℂm\displaystyle\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}\}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{n},~\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{r}\}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{m}

such that

X=∑i=1rσi​(X)​Ri, where ​Ri=ui​vi∗.X=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}(X)R_{i},\text{~where~}R_{i}=u_{i}v_{i}^{*}.

ci​(εi)=1+εi​si2,c_{i}(\varepsilon_{i})=\frac{1+\varepsilon_{i}s_{i}}{2}, (8)

pε=∏i=1rci​(εi).p_{\varepsilon}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}c_{i}(\varepsilon_{i}). (9)

Proposition 2.9.
∑ε∈Ωrpε=1.\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}=1.

With these preliminaries, we now establish the following results.

Lemma 2.10.

Let D∈Mn,m​(ℂ)D\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}) be a contraction and r=min⁡{m,n}r=\min\{m,n\}. If a singular value decomposition ∑i=1rσi​(D)​Ri\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}(D)R_{i} of DD is fixed, then

D=∑ε∈Ωrpε​Qε,D=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}Q_{\varepsilon}, (10)

where pε=∏i=1r1+εi​σi​(D)2≥0p_{\varepsilon}=\prod_{i=1}^{r}\frac{1+\varepsilon_{i}\sigma_{i}(D)}{2}\geq 0, ε=(ε1,…,εr)∈Ωr\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{r})\in\Omega_{r}, ∑ε∈Ωrpε=1\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}=1, and

Qε=∑i=1rεi​Ri.Q_{\varepsilon}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\varepsilon_{i}R_{i}. (11)

Moreover, (11) has the following properties:

  1. (i)

    If σj​(D)<1\sigma_{j}(D)<1, and ε+\varepsilon^{+} and ε−\varepsilon^{-} are defined as in Remark 2.8, then

    Qε+−Qε−=2​Rj.Q_{\varepsilon^{+}}-Q_{\varepsilon^{-}}=2R_{j}. (12)
  2. (ii)

    If n≥mn\geq m, then for every ε∈Ωr\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}, QεQ_{\varepsilon} is an isometric matrix.

  3. (iii)

    If n<mn<m, then for every ε∈Ωr\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}, QεQ_{\varepsilon} is a coisometric matrix.

Proof.

Since DD is a contraction, we have 0≤σi​(D)≤1​(i=1,…,r).0\leq\sigma_{i}(D)\leq 1~(i=1,\ldots,r). Thus, by (8) and (9), pεp_{\varepsilon} satisfies the required definition. By Remark 2.8 and Proposition 2.9, pε≥0p_{\varepsilon}\geq 0 for every ε∈Ωr\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}, and ∑ε∈Ωrpε=1\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}=1. We next prove (10). By (11) and finite additivity,

∑ε∈Ωrpε​Qε\displaystyle\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}Q_{\varepsilon} =∑ε∈Ωrpε​(∑i=1rεi​Ri)\displaystyle=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\varepsilon_{i}R_{i}\right)
=∑i=1r(∑ε∈Ωrpε​εi)​Ri\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\left(\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}\varepsilon_{i}\right)R_{i}
=∑i=1rσi​(D)​Ri​(by Proposition 2.9)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}(D)R_{i}~(\text{by Proposition~\ref{prop:sign-weight-moments}})
=D.\displaystyle=D.

Qε+−Qε−\displaystyle Q_{\varepsilon^{+}}-Q_{\varepsilon^{-}} =∑i=1r(εi+−εi−)​Ri\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\left(\varepsilon_{i}^{+}-\varepsilon_{i}^{-}\right)R_{i}
=(εj+−εj−)​Rj\displaystyle=\left(\varepsilon_{j}^{+}-\varepsilon_{j}^{-}\right)R_{j}
=2​Rj.\displaystyle=2R_{j}.

Thus, (12) holds. By (11),

Qε=∑i=1rεi​ui​vi∗.Q_{\varepsilon}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\varepsilon_{i}u_{i}v_{i}^{*}.

First assume n≥mn\geq m. Then r=mr=m, {u1,…,ur}⊆ℂn\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}\}\subseteq\mathbb{C}^{n} is an orthonormal set, and

v1,…,vmv_{1},\ldots,v_{m}

form an orthonormal basis of ℂm\mathbb{C}^{m}. Hence,

Qε∗​Qε\displaystyle Q_{\varepsilon}^{*}Q_{\varepsilon} =(∑i=1mεi​vi​ui∗)​(∑j=1mεj​uj​vj∗)\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{i}v_{i}u_{i}^{*}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{j}u_{j}v_{j}^{*}\right)

=∑i=1mεi2​vi​vi∗\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{i}^{2}v_{i}v_{i}^{*}
=Im​(since ​εi2=1).\displaystyle=I_{m}~(\text{since }\varepsilon_{i}^{2}=1).

Thus, QεQ_{\varepsilon} is an isometric matrix.

Now assume n<mn<m. The same argument shows that QεQ_{\varepsilon} is a coisometric matrix. In particular, when m=nm=n, every QεQ_{\varepsilon} is a unitary matrix. ∎

The following result is important for proving that (3) holds and for characterizing the necessary and sufficient condition for equality in it.

Lemma 2.11.

Let NN be a positive integer, let p1,…,pNp_{1},\ldots,p_{N} be nonnegative real numbers such that ∑i=1Npi=1,\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}=1, and let X1,…,XN∈Mm,n​(ℂ)X_{1},\ldots,X_{N}\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}). Then

‖∑i=1Npi​Xi‖F2≤∑i=1Npi​‖Xi‖F2.\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\left\lVert X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (13)

Equality holds in (13) if and only if Xi=XjX_{i}=X_{j} for any i,ji,j such that pi>0p_{i}>0 and pj>0p_{j}>0.

Proof.

For any i,ji,j,

‖Xi−Xj‖F2\displaystyle\left\lVert X_{i}-X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2} =‖Xi‖F2+‖Xj‖F2−2​Re⁡(Xi,Xj),\displaystyle=\left\lVert X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\left\lVert X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}-2\operatorname{Re}\left(X_{i},X_{j}\right),

where Re⁡(X,Y)=12​((X,Y)+(Y,X)).\operatorname{Re}\left(X,Y\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\left(X,Y\right)+\left(Y,X\right)\right). Hence,

12​∑i,j=1Npi​pj​‖Xi−Xj‖F2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{i}-X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
=12​∑i,j=1Npi​pj​‖Xi‖F2+12​∑i,j=1Npi​pj​‖Xj‖F2−∑i,j=1Npi​pj​Re⁡(Xi,Xj).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}-\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\operatorname{Re}\left(X_{i},X_{j}\right).

For the first term, using ∑j=1Npj=1\sum_{j=1}^{N}p_{j}=1, we obtain

12​∑i,j=1Npi​pj​‖Xi‖F2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2} =12​∑i=1Npi​‖Xi‖F2​∑j=1Npj\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\left\lVert X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}p_{j}
=12​∑i=1Npi​‖Xi‖F2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\left\lVert X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

Similarly, the second term satisfies

12​∑i,j=1Npi​pj​‖Xj‖F2\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2} =12​∑j=1Npj​‖Xj‖F2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

Thus, the sum of the first two terms is

∑i=1Npi​‖Xi‖F2.\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\left\lVert X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

For the inner-product term, since pip_{i} and pjp_{j} are real numbers,

∑i,j=1Npi​pj​(Xi,Xj)\displaystyle\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left(X_{i},X_{j}\right) =(∑i=1Npi​Xi,∑j=1Npj​Xj)\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}X_{i},\sum_{j=1}^{N}p_{j}X_{j}\right)
=‖∑i=1Npi​Xi‖F2.\displaystyle=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

Since ‖∑i=1Npi​Xi‖F2\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2} is real,

∑i,j=1Npi​pj​Re⁡(Xi,Xj)\displaystyle\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\operatorname{Re}\left(X_{i},X_{j}\right) =Re∑i,j=1Npipj(Xi,Xj)\displaystyle=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left(X_{i},X_{j}\right)
=‖∑i=1Npi​Xi‖F2.\displaystyle=\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

Therefore,

∑i=1Npi​‖Xi‖F2−‖∑i=1Npi​Xi‖F2=12​∑i,j=1Npi​pj​‖Xi−Xj‖F2.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\left\lVert X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}-\left\lVert\sum_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}X_{i}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{i}-X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (14)

Every term on the right-hand side of (14) is nonnegative. Therefore, (13) holds.

Finally, we discuss the equality condition. By (14), equality holds in (13) if and only if

12​∑i,j=1Npi​pj​‖Xi−Xj‖F2=0.\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}p_{i}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{i}-X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=0.

This holds exactly when

pi​pj​‖Xi−Xj‖F2=0,p_{i}p_{j}\left\lVert X_{i}-X_{j}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=0,

which in turn holds precisely when Xi=XjX_{i}=X_{j} for any pi>0p_{i}>0 and pj>0p_{j}>0. ∎

3 Proof of Conjecture 1.1

In this section, we first give a complete proof of Conjecture 1.1, and then show that the constant 22 in (3) is optimal for every fixed m,n≥2m,n\geq 2.

Theorem 3.1.

Let m,n≥2m,n\geq 2, A,C∈Mm,n​(ℂ)A,C\in M_{m,n}(\mathbb{C}), and B∈Mn,m​(ℂ)B\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}). Then (3) holds.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1, it suffices to prove that (5) holds. First assume n≥mn\geq m. By Lemma 2.10, there exist pε≥0p_{\varepsilon}\geq 0 and isometric matrices QεQ_{\varepsilon} such that

D=∑εpε​Qε,∑εpε=1,Qε∗​Qε=Im.D=\sum_{\varepsilon}p_{\varepsilon}Q_{\varepsilon},~\sum_{\varepsilon}p_{\varepsilon}=1,~Q_{\varepsilon}^{*}Q_{\varepsilon}=I_{m}.

By the linearity of Φ\Phi,

Φ⁡(D)=∑εpε​Φ​(Qε),\Phi(D)=\sum_{\varepsilon}p_{\varepsilon}\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon}),

where Φ⁡(Qε)=A​Qε​C−C​Qε​A\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})=AQ_{\varepsilon}C-CQ_{\varepsilon}A. By Lemma 2.11,

‖Φ⁡(D)‖F2\displaystyle\left\lVert\Phi(D)\right\rVert_{F}^{2} ≤∑εpε​‖Φ⁡(Qε)‖F2.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\varepsilon}p_{\varepsilon}\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

By Lemma 2.5, for every ε\varepsilon,

‖Φ⁡(Qε)‖F2≤2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\leq 2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (15)

Therefore,

‖Φ⁡(D)‖F2\displaystyle\left\lVert\Phi(D)\right\rVert_{F}^{2} ≤∑εpε​(2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\varepsilon}p_{\varepsilon}\left(2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\right)
=2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\displaystyle=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

This proves the case n≥mn\geq m. If m>nm>n, Lemma 2.10 writes DD as a convex combination of coisometric matrices. We then use the coisometric case of Lemma 2.5; the remaining steps are the same. Thus, (3) holds. ∎

Remark 3.2.

Since Theorem 3.1 proves Conjecture 1.1, the implication established by Nobori immediately yields (4).

Next, we show that the constant 22 is optimal.

Proposition 3.3.

For every fixed m,n≥2m,n\geq 2, the constant 22 in (3) is best possible.

Proof.

It is enough to give, for each fixed (m,n)(m,n), an example for which the constant 22 is attained. Let

A2=[100−1],C2=[0100].A_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&-1\end{bmatrix},~C_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix}.

A direct calculation gives

A2​C2−C2​A2=[0200],A_{2}C_{2}-C_{2}A_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0&2\\ 0&0\end{bmatrix},

so

‖A2​C2−C2​A2‖F2=4.\left\lVert A_{2}C_{2}-C_{2}A_{2}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=4. (16)

Also,

‖A2‖(2),22=12+12=2,‖C2‖F2=1.\left\lVert A_{2}\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}=1^{2}+1^{2}=2,~\left\lVert C_{2}\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=1.

Case (a): n≥mn\geq m. Let

B=[Im𝟎(n−m)×m]∈Mn,m​(ℂ).B=\begin{bmatrix}I_{m}\\ \mathbf{0}_{(n-m)\times m}\end{bmatrix}\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}).

Clearly,

B∗​B=Im,‖B‖2=1.B^{*}B=I_{m},~\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}=1.

Construct the m×mm\times m matrices

A^=[A2𝟎𝟎𝟎m−2]​C^=[C2𝟎𝟎𝟎m−2],\widehat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}A_{2}&\mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}&\mathbf{0}_{m-2}\end{bmatrix}~\widehat{C}=\begin{bmatrix}C_{2}&\mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}&\mathbf{0}_{m-2}\end{bmatrix},

and let

A=[A^𝟎m×(n−m)],C=[C^𝟎m×(n−m)].A=\begin{bmatrix}\widehat{A}&\mathbf{0}_{m\times(n-m)}\end{bmatrix},~C=\begin{bmatrix}\widehat{C}&\mathbf{0}_{m\times(n-m)}\end{bmatrix}.

Then

A​B​C−C​B​A\displaystyle ABC-CBA =[A^​C^−C^​A^𝟎].\displaystyle=\begin{bmatrix}\widehat{A}\widehat{C}-\widehat{C}\widehat{A}&\mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}.

Its only possibly nonzero upper-left 2×22\times 2 block is A2​C2−C2​A2A_{2}C_{2}-C_{2}A_{2}. Hence, by (16),

‖A​B​C−C​B​A‖F2=4.\left\lVert ABC-CBA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=4.

On the other hand, adding zero columns to the right does not change the nonzero singular values. Therefore,

‖A‖(2),22=2,‖C‖F2=1.\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}=2,~\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=1.

Thus, equality holds.

Case (b): n<mn<m. Let

B=[In𝟎n×(m−n)]∈Mn,m​(ℂ).B=\begin{bmatrix}I_{n}&\mathbf{0}_{n\times(m-n)}\end{bmatrix}\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}).

Then

B​B∗=In,‖B‖2=1.BB^{*}=I_{n},~\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}=1.

Construct

A~=[A2𝟎𝟎𝟎n−2],C~=[C2𝟎𝟎𝟎n−2],\widetilde{A}=\begin{bmatrix}A_{2}&\mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}&\mathbf{0}_{n-2}\end{bmatrix},~\widetilde{C}=\begin{bmatrix}C_{2}&\mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}&\mathbf{0}_{n-2}\end{bmatrix},

and let

A=[A~𝟎(m−n)×n],C=[C~𝟎(m−n)×n].A=\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{A}\\ \mathbf{0}_{(m-n)\times n}\end{bmatrix},~C=\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{C}\\ \mathbf{0}_{(m-n)\times n}\end{bmatrix}.

Then

A​B​C−C​B​A=[A~​C~−C~​A~𝟎].ABC-CBA=\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde{A}\widetilde{C}-\widetilde{C}\widetilde{A}\\ \mathbf{0}\end{bmatrix}.

As in the previous case, we obtain

‖A​B​C−C​B​A‖F2=4,‖A‖(2),22=2,‖C‖F2=1,‖B‖22=1.\left\lVert ABC-CBA\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=4,~\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}=2,~\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=1,~\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=1.

Thus, equality holds. ∎

4 Necessary and Sufficient Conditions for Equality

We now give an equality criterion for (3).

Theorem 4.1.

Let D=B‖B‖2∈Mn,m​(ℂ)D=\frac{B}{\left\lVert B\right\rVert_{2}}\in M_{n,m}(\mathbb{C}) and r=min⁡{m,n}r=\min\{m,n\}. If a singular value decomposition ∑i=1rσi​(D)​Ri\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}(D)R_{i} of DD is fixed, then equality holds in (3) if and only if the following two conditions hold:

(a) For every index ii such that σi​(D)<1\sigma_{i}(D)<1,

A​Ri​C=C​Ri​A.AR_{i}C=CR_{i}A.

(b) Let Q𝟏=∑i=1rRiQ_{\bm{1}}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}R_{i} be constructed from the all-one vector 𝟏\bm{1} as in Lemma 2.10. If n≥mn\geq m, then

‖(Q𝟏​A)​(Q𝟏​C)−(Q𝟏​C)​(Q𝟏​A)‖F2=2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\left\lVert(Q_{\bm{1}}A)(Q_{\bm{1}}C)-(Q_{\bm{1}}C)(Q_{\bm{1}}A)\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

If m>nm>n, then

‖(A​Q𝟏)​(C​Q𝟏)−(C​Q𝟏)​(A​Q𝟏)‖F2=2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\left\lVert(AQ_{\bm{1}})(CQ_{\bm{1}})-(CQ_{\bm{1}})(AQ_{\bm{1}})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.
Proof.

If n≥mn\geq m, then Qε∗​Qε=ImQ_{\varepsilon}^{*}Q_{\varepsilon}=I_{m}, while if m>nm>n, then Qε​Qε∗=InQ_{\varepsilon}Q_{\varepsilon}^{*}=I_{n}. Therefore, Lemma 2.5 gives (15) in both cases. By Lemma 2.1, equality in (3) is equivalent to

‖Φ⁡(D)‖F2=2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\left\lVert\Phi(D)\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (17)

By Lemma 2.10,

D=∑ε∈Ωrpε​Qε,pε≥0,∑ε∈Ωrpε=1.D=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}Q_{\varepsilon},~p_{\varepsilon}\geq 0,~\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}=1.

By the proof of Theorem 3.1,

‖Φ⁡(D)‖F2\displaystyle\left\lVert\Phi(D)\right\rVert_{F}^{2} ≤∑ε∈Ωrpε​‖Φ⁡(Qε)‖F2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})\right\rVert_{F}^{2} (18)
≤2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\displaystyle\leq 2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

We now prove necessity and sufficiency separately.

Assume that equality holds in (3). By (17) and (18),

∑ε∈Ωrpε​‖Φ⁡(Qε)‖F2=2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (19)

By (15), for every ε∈Ωr\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r},

2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2−‖Φ⁡(Qε)‖F2≥0.2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}-\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\geq 0.

Together with (19), this gives

0\displaystyle 0 =2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2−∑ε∈Ωrpε​‖Φ⁡(Qε)‖F2\displaystyle=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}-\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}
=∑ε∈Ωrpε​(2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2−‖Φ⁡(Qε)‖F2).\displaystyle=\sum_{\varepsilon\in\Omega_{r}}p_{\varepsilon}\left(2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}-\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}\right).

The right-hand side is a finite sum of nonnegative numbers. Therefore, whenever pε>0p_{\varepsilon}>0,

‖Φ⁡(Qε)‖F2=2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (20)

Also, the first inequality in (18) must be an equality. By the equality condition in Lemma 2.11,

Φ⁡(Qε)=Φ⁡(Qδ)​whenever ​pε>0​ and ​pδ>0.\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon})=\Phi(Q_{\delta})~\text{whenever }p_{\varepsilon}>0\text{ and }p_{\delta}>0. (21)

Now fix an index ii such that σi​(D)<1\sigma_{i}(D)<1. By Lemma 2.10, there are two sign vectors ε+,ε−∈Ωr\varepsilon^{+},\varepsilon^{-}\in\Omega_{r} such that pε+>0,pε−>0,p_{\varepsilon^{+}}>0,~p_{\varepsilon^{-}}>0, and

Qε+−Qε−=2​Ri.Q_{\varepsilon^{+}}-Q_{\varepsilon^{-}}=2R_{i}. (22)

By (21),

Φ⁡(Qε+)=Φ⁡(Qε−).\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon^{+}})=\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon^{-}}).

Using the linearity of Φ\Phi and (22),

0\displaystyle 0 =Φ⁡(Qε+)−Φ⁡(Qε−)\displaystyle=\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon^{+}})-\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon^{-}})
=Φ⁡(Qε+−Qε−)\displaystyle=\Phi(Q_{\varepsilon^{+}}-Q_{\varepsilon^{-}})
=Φ⁡(2​Ri).\displaystyle=\Phi(2R_{i}).

This proves condition (a). We next prove condition (b). By Lemma 2.10, p𝟏>0.p_{\bm{1}}>0. Hence, by (20),

‖Φ⁡(Q𝟏)‖F2=2​‖A‖(2),22​‖C‖F2.\left\lVert\Phi(Q_{\bm{1}})\right\rVert_{F}^{2}=2\left\lVert A\right\rVert_{(2),2}^{2}\left\lVert C\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. (23)

Thus, condition (b) holds, by (6) and (7).

Now assume that conditions (a) and (b) both hold. First, (23) holds. Also,

Φ⁡(D)−Φ⁡(Q𝟏)\displaystyle\Phi(D)-\Phi(Q_{\bm{1}}) =Φ⁡(∑i=1rσi​(D)​Ri−∑i=1rRi)\displaystyle=\Phi\left(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}(D)R_{i}-\sum_{i=1}^{r}R_{i}\right)
=∑i=1r(σi​(D)−1)​Φ​(Ri).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\bigl(\sigma_{i}(D)-1\bigr)\Phi(R_{i}).

If σi​(D)=1\sigma_{i}(D)=1, then (σi​(D)−1)​Φ​(Ri)=0.\bigl(\sigma_{i}(D)-1\bigr)\Phi(R_{i})=0. If σi​(D)<1\sigma_{i}(D)<1, then by condition (a),

Φ⁡(Ri)=A​Ri​C−C​Ri​A=0,\Phi(R_{i})=AR_{i}C-CR_{i}A=0,

so again (σi​(D)−1)​Φ​(Ri)=0.\bigl(\sigma_{i}(D)-1\bigr)\Phi(R_{i})=0. Therefore, Φ⁡(D)=Φ⁡(Q𝟏).\Phi(D)=\Phi(Q_{\bm{1}}). Hence, (17) holds, which proves sufficiency. ∎

Remark 4.2.

Condition (b) is precisely the equality condition for Böttcher–Wenzel inequality (2), as characterized in [3]. In particular, when all singular values of DD are 11, condition (a) is absent. In this case, the equality condition reduces to that of the Böttcher–Wenzel inequality [3].
